stem: Mains conducted emissions are a measurement of:
choices: Radiated power from the antenna port
RF voltage between each power conductor and ground
explanation: The limit is a terminal voltage, not a field. Part 15 and ICES-003 both take it from each line to ground through a line-impedance network.

stem: The usual mains frequency window for this test is:
explanation: Section 15.107, ICES-003 Table 1, and EN 301 489-1 clause 8.4 all use 150 kHz to 30 MHz on the AC mains.

stem: The LISN (AMN) specified for Part 15 mains measurements is:
choices: 50 µH in series with a 50 Ω measurement port
explanation: Sections 15.31(l) and 15.107 call it a 50 µH/50 ohm network. CISPR 16-1-2 is the usual home of that AMN definition.

stem: Both of these detectors must be satisfied on a mains conducted limit unless a rule gives a shortcut:
explanation: The tables print a quasi-peak column and an average column. Meeting one column does not retire the other, except for the shortcut below.

stem: EN 301 489-1 allows you to skip the average detector when:
choices: The quasi-peak reading is already under the average limit
The cable is shorter than 3 m
The peak reading is under the quasi-peak limit
explanation: Clauses 8.3.3 and 8.4.3.1 say a quasi-peak result that meets the average limit covers both, because quasi-peak will not read lower than average.

stem: Class B conducted limits from 0.5 MHz to 5 MHz in §15.107(a) are:
explanation: That middle band is flat at 56 and 46. The band below it slopes, and the band above it steps up to 60 and 50.

stem: Class B conducted limits from 5 MHz to 30 MHz in §15.107(a) are:
explanation: The top band of the Class B table is 60 dBµV quasi-peak and 50 dBµV average. ICES-003 Table 1 Class B matches those same three rows.

stem: From 150 kHz to 500 kHz the Class B quasi-peak limit:
choices: Falls from 66 dBµV to 56 dBµV as the log of frequency rises
explanation: The star note says the limit decreases with the logarithm of frequency. The average limit falls from 56 dBµV to 46 dBµV over the same span.

stem: At the 5 MHz boundary of the Class B table, the quasi-peak limit that applies is:
choices: 56 dBµV, the lower of the two meeting values
explanation: Section 15.107(a) says the lower limit applies at the band edges. 56 dBµV is tighter than 60 dBµV.

stem: Class A conducted limits from 0.15 MHz to 0.5 MHz in §15.107(b) are:
explanation: Class A does not slope in that first segment. From 0.5 MHz to 30 MHz the Class A pair is 73 and 60.

stem: Class A conducted limits from 0.5 MHz to 30 MHz in §15.107(b) are:
explanation: One pair covers that whole span for Class A. ICES-003 prints the same 73/60 numbers in both the 0.5–5 MHz row and the 5–30 MHz row.

stem: A battery-only product skips the Part 15 conducted test when:
choices: It never operates from AC and has no provision for AC operation
It is powered through another device that is plugged in
It includes a charger that allows use while charging
explanation: Section 15.107(d) draws that line. Chargers, adaptors, battery eliminators, and indirect AC power all bring the conducted test back.

stem: Which line do you measure?
choices: Each mains conductor to ground, not line-to-line as the reported result
explanation: Compliance is the voltage between each power line and ground at the power terminal. A quiet neutral does not excuse a noisy live conductor.

stem: An unused RF port on the LISN is:
explanation: An open measurement port changes the impedance the product sees. ICES-002 says the same thing for unused AMN and ISN ports: fit 50 Ω terminations.

stem: The usual CISPR bandwidth from 150 kHz to 30 MHz is:
explanation: That is CISPR band B in CISPR 16-1-1. Using 120 kHz or 1 MHz here makes the reading incomparable to the limit.

stem: The usual tabletop mains arrangement in ANSI C63.4 and CISPR 16-2-1 practice is:
choices: About 40 cm from the vertical reference plane and about 80 cm from the LISN
The EUT sitting on the LISN
explanation: Those two spacings are the textbook picture. Bond the LISN to the reference plane, and if the method you cited uses different numbers, follow that method and write them down.

stem: Excess mains lead should be:
choices: Dressed so it does not become a coil, often as a serpentine or z-fold
Replaced with a longer unshielded extension of unknown origin
explanation: A coil adds impedance and can hide noise or move a resonance. ICES-002 gives one concrete version for a vehicle charge cable: z-fold, no wider than 50 cm, on insulating supports up to 15 cm.

stem: ICES-002 places the AMN laterally:
choices: 80 cm from the vehicle, +20 cm / −0 cm
explanation: That 80 cm (+20/−0) spacing is in §4.3.2.2, with the AMN bonded to the ground plane. It is not the 40 cm vertical-plane spacing used for tabletop ITE.

stem: You measure the mode that:
choices: Produces the largest emission consistent with intended use
explanation: EN 301 489-1 clause 8.1.2 and the Part 15 maximize rule agree. Record the mode, and a charger should be charging, not sitting idle, if charging is the noisy intended use.

stem: A support laptop plugged into the same LISN as the product:
choices: Can be the source of the noise you assign to the product
explanation: If the laptop is not part of the product, give it its own filtered supply or a second network. Otherwise you fail the product for the laptop.

stem: Measuring on the mains side of the LISN instead of the EUT port:
choices: Is the wrong side of the network and is not the compliance voltage
Removes the need for a ground bond
explanation: The EUT port is the defined impedance. The mains connector is the utility side, and swapping them invalidates the limit comparison.

stem: A floating bond between the LISN and the reference plane:
choices: Is the preferred Class B setup
Changes the impedance and usually raises or destabilizes the reading
explanation: The network is defined with its ground strapped to the plane. A paint gap or a long ground wire is a classic fail.

stem: Peak detector on a conducted scan is:
choices: A search tool, not automatically the quasi-peak result
The detector the §15.107 limit is written in
explanation: The limit columns are quasi-peak and average. A peak pass can be conservative, and a peak fail still needs the detector the limit names.

stem: Quasi-peak reads lower than peak when:
choices: The noise is a pure continuous sine
The noise is impulsive and has a low repetition rate
explanation: The quasi-peak time constants weight repetition rate. Clicks can look illegal on peak and legal on quasi-peak, and a continuous tone barely moves between the two.

stem: Telecom or network ports use a coupling network that is:
choices: An ISN or CDN sized for that cable, not the mains LISN
explanation: ICES-002 uses an ISN when communication wires ride in the AC harness, and a LISN on the mains conductors. The two are not interchangeable.

stem: IEC 61000-6-3 in this pack is:
choices: A preview. Do not quote numeric mains limits from it
explanation: The preview lists Table 4 for the low-voltage AC mains port and does not print the numbers. Use FCC, ICES, or the full standard you actually own.

stem: The IEC 61000-6-3 preview says to test:
choices: Every table row, even with no connector
Only the ports that exist on the equipment
explanation: Clause 7 of the preview limits the work to ports that are present, while the test plan still has to consider each applicable row.

stem: CISPR 14-1, from the preview, separates:
explanation: The contents list continuous disturbances and discontinuous disturbances, including a click analyser. The preview does not include the click-rate numbers, so they are not quizzed here.

stem: EN 301 489-1 Table 5, DC conducted, 0.5 MHz to 30 MHz, is:
explanation: Table 5 is 79/66 from 0.15–0.5 MHz and 73/60 from 0.5–30 MHz. It is not the Class B mains shape.

stem: DC conducted emissions in EN 301 489-1 apply when the DC cable to a local DC network is:
explanation: At or under 3 m, and going to a dedicated AC/DC supply, the measurement moves to that supply's AC port. Longer than 3 m, you also measure the DC port.

stem: ICES-002 Class B conducted limits from 0.15 MHz to 0.5 MHz:
choices: Slope from 66 to 56 dBµV quasi-peak and from 56 to 46 dBµV average
explanation: Table 2 of ICES-002 is the residential shape, including the log slope. Class A in Table 1 is the power-rated table and is a different set of numbers.

stem: A Class A vehicle supply rated 10 kW, under ICES-002 Table 1 from 0.15–0.5 MHz, is limited to:
explanation: 10 kW is under the 20 kVA column. The 100/90 pair is only for the mid-power column, and only when its installation notes are met.

stem: If that higher-power Class A product can be plugged into low-voltage overhead lines, ICES-002 says to use:
explanation: Note iv says the relaxed mid-power limits are not for low-voltage overhead lines. If that connection is possible, fall back to the ≤ 20 kVA limits.

stem: ICES-003 Class A from 5 MHz to 30 MHz is:
explanation: The Class A 5–30 MHz cell matches the 0.5–5 MHz cell. Class B steps up to 60/50 in that top band.

stem: The more stringent limit at a transition frequency means:
choices: Use the lower of the two values that meet at that frequency
Use the average of the two
explanation: Both ICES-003 and ICES-002 say the more stringent limit applies at transitions. Part 15 says the lower limit applies at the band edges, and same idea.

stem: A reading of 62 dBµV quasi-peak at 1 MHz on a Class B mains port is:
choices: Ignored because it is above 500 kHz
A fail against the 56 dBµV quasi-peak limit
Compared with the Class A 79 dBµV limit by default
explanation: From 0.5 MHz to 5 MHz the Class B quasi-peak limit is 56 dBµV. 62 is over it, whatever the average reading does.

stem: A reading of 44 dBµV average at 1 MHz on a Class B mains port is:
choices: A pass against the 46 dBµV average limit
explanation: The average limit in that band is 46 dBµV. 44 is under it, and you still owe the quasi-peak comparison unless the quasi-peak reading already sat under 46.

stem: A reading of 70 dBµV quasi-peak at 200 kHz, Class B, needs the sloping limit. The limit at 200 kHz is:
choices: There is no limit below 500 kHz
Between 66 dBµV and 56 dBµV, computed from the log of frequency
explanation: The first band slopes. You interpolate with the log of frequency between the endpoints, and you do not apply the 0.5 MHz endpoint at 200 kHz.

stem: Carrier-current systems that keep their fundamental in 535–1705 kHz and are meant for an AM broadcast receiver:
explanation: That one case has no conducted limit. Other carrier-current systems in that band are held to 1000 µV on a 50 µH/50 Ω LISN, and radiated limits still apply.

stem: Other carrier-current systems, in 535–1705 kHz, are limited to:
choices: 1000 µV on a 50 µH/50 Ω LISN
explanation: Section 15.107(c)(2) is the 1000 µV rule. They also follow the radiated rules cited in §15.109(e).

stem: If the product has no AC mains port and no external supply, mains conducted:
choices: Does not apply, because there is no port to measure
Is performed on a dummy plug
explanation: The IEC 61000-6-3 preview says you measure ports that exist. Part 15 says the same thing for a pure battery device with no AC provision.

stem: PoE or another external supply, under ICES-003, moves the conducted limit to:
choices: The Ethernet wires only, with no mains measurement
The AC mains of that external device while it powers the ITE
explanation: Section 3.2.1 is explicit. You do not skip mains conducted just because the brick is a separate box, if the brick is what plugs into the wall.

stem: Harmonic-current limits are not the same test as mains conducted RF. In EN 301 489-1, up to 16 A per phase, harmonics come from:
explanation: Clause 8.5 points at EN 61000-3-2 up to 16 A, and EN 61000-3-12 above that up to 75 A. Flicker is yet another table, EN 61000-3-3 or EN 61000-3-11.

stem: A conducted plot with no ground-plane bond and no 50 Ω terminations is:
choices: Not a compliance result, even if the trace looks low
explanation: The limit assumes the network and the bond. A pretty trace from a broken setup does not go in the report as a pass.

stem: Average detector versus quasi-peak on a continuous tone:
choices: Quasi-peak is not used on mains
They nearly agree, so a large gap is a clue that something is impulsive or the setup is wrong
explanation: On CW they should be close. A big split means clicks, bursts, or a detector setting you did not mean to use.

stem: ICES-002 Table 1 for Class A above 75 kVA, 5–30 MHz, is:
explanation: The >75 kVA column is 130/120, then 125/115, then 115/105. Those limits also demand the dedicated-supply and separation conditions in note v.

stem: The >75 kVA conducted limits in ICES-002 may be used only when, among other things:
choices: The installation is at least 30 m from residences or behind a barrier, on a dedicated transformer or generator, not on overhead lines
explanation: Note v lists the dedicated supply, the 30 m or barrier separation, and the installation instructions. Missing any of that drops you back down the table.

stem: Report the conducted result with:
choices: A single number and no setup
The limit, the detector, the line, the network, and the operating mode
explanation: The next person has to be able to repeat the comparison. ICES-003 also wants the chosen radiated method in the report, but the conducted rows still need their own conditions.

stem: A preselector or a pulsed limiter in the conducted path:
choices: Must be accounted for, because it can change the quasi-peak and average readings
explanation: Anything between the LISN port and the detector is part of the measurement chain. An uncalibrated limiter is a good way to buy a false pass.

stem: Class B at 10 MHz, quasi-peak limit, is:
explanation: 10 MHz sits in the 5–30 MHz row. Quasi-peak is 60 dBµV and average is 50 dBµV, and 56 dBµV is the middle-band quasi-peak limit.

stem: Class B at 300 kHz, the quasi-peak limit is:
choices: On the slope between 66 dBµV and 56 dBµV
explanation: 300 kHz is inside 0.15–0.5 MHz. Both the quasi-peak and the average limits are still moving with the log of frequency.

stem: Switching the product off and watching the trace is how you:
choices: Choose Class A versus Class B
Separate ambient and LISN leakage from the product
explanation: If the spur stays with the product off, it is not the product. Fix the bond, the termination, or the supply filter before you write a failure.

stem: Class A mains limits are:
choices: Higher (looser) than Class B, and they are for equipment that is not marketed for the home
The same numbers at a different distance
explanation: Compare 79/66 and 73/60 with the Class B slope and the 56/46 and 60/50 steps. Class A is the commercial table, and it is not a free upgrade for a home product.

stem: EN 301 489-1 AC mains conducted limits for ordinary fixed equipment are:
choices: The EN 55032 Class B mains limits, or Class A if the equipment is only for industry or a telecom centre
explanation: Clause 8.4.3.2 points at EN 55032 Class B, with Class A as the industrial or telecom-centre alternative. The frequency window is still 150 kHz to 30 MHz.

stem: In-home PLC on the AC port between 1.6 MHz and 30 MHz, in EN 301 489-1, is judged against:
choices: EN 50561-1 instead of the ordinary mains limits
explanation: Clause 8.4.3.3 swaps in EN 50561-1 for that PLC band, and EN 50561-3 when the PLC is above 30 MHz. Do not force the ordinary Class B mains table onto that port.

stem: The LISN's job is to:
choices: Present a defined RF impedance and pass the disturbance voltage to the receiver
explanation: Without a stable impedance the dBµV number is not the quantity in the table. That is why the bond and the 50 Ω terminations are part of the test, not accessories.

stem: dBµV is:
explanation: Conducted limits in these tables are voltages, so the unit is dBµV. Radiated tables that say dBµV/m are a different quantity.

stem: 66 dBµV is:
explanation: dBµV = 20·log10(V in µV). 66 dBµV is 10^(66/20) µV, about 2000 µV, or 2 mV, and do not treat it as a field.

stem: A product marketed for the home is not saved by a quiet chamber if the mains fail, because:
choices: Class B has no conducted limit
The LISN is optional for Class B
Conducted and radiated are separate requirements
explanation: Section 15.107 applies to equipment designed to connect to the AC line, Class A or Class B. A clean 3 m plot does not retire it.

stem: Common fail: testing only one mains conductor.
choices: The standard says to pick the quieter line
The other conductor can be the one over the limit
explanation: The rule is each line to ground. Record both, and the worse one is the result.

stem: AMN and LISN in these documents:
choices: Are the same kind of network; ICES says AMN, Part 15 says LISN
Are different tests with different frequency ranges
explanation: ICES-002 and ICES-003 use 'artificial mains network'. Part 15 uses 'line impedance stabilization network', and for this mains test they are the 50 µH/50 Ω device.

stem: A Class B average reading of 48 dBµV at 8 MHz is:
explanation: 8 MHz is in 5–30 MHz, where the average limit is 50 dBµV. The 46 dBµV average limit belongs to 0.5–5 MHz, and check the quasi-peak column separately.

stem: The ground plane under a conducted setup is:
choices: Part of the defined impedance, not optional furniture
A safety earth with no RF job
explanation: The LISN and the vertical reference plane only work as specified when they are bonded. A wooden bench with a floating brick is a different test.

stem: Do not invent a conducted limit from:
choices: A preview contents page that names a table but does not print it
explanation: The preview of IEC 61000-6-3 names the AC, DC, and wired-port tables. The numbers you are allowed to memorize are the ones printed in the full texts in this pack.

stem: ICES-003 Class B quasi-peak from 0.15 MHz to 0.5 MHz:
choices: Is a peak limit of 74 dBµV
Decreases linearly with the log of frequency from 66 dBµV to 56 dBµV
explanation: Table 1's note says the level decreases linearly with the logarithm of frequency. The average column does the same from 56 to 46.

stem: If charging current is adjustable, ICES-002 conducted tests on a plug-in vehicle set it to:
choices: At least 80% of maximum for the whole test
explanation: Section 4.3.2.1 wants at least 80% when you can set the current. If you cannot, hold battery state of charge between 20% and 80%.

stem: A conducted failure at one frequency is still a failure when:
choices: It is over the limit in the detector the limit uses, on either line
The rest of the plot is 20 dB under
The operator prefers the average trace
explanation: The limit is a limit at each frequency, not an average across the plot. One over-limit point fails the comparison.

stem: CISPR band A, 9 kHz to 150 kHz, uses a narrower bandwidth than band B. The usual figure is:
explanation: Band B at 9 kHz starts at 150 kHz, which is where these mains limits start. Below that, band A at 200 Hz is the CISPR 16-1-1 practice, and do not carry 9 kHz down into band A.

stem: A 1000 µV carrier-current limit is about:
explanation: 1000 µV is 60 dBµV, because 20·log10(1000) = 60. That is the §15.107(c)(2) number, not the Class B 60 dBµV quasi-peak cell, though the decibel value matches.

stem: At 0.2 MHz, which Class B conducted statement is right?
choices: Class A 73/60 applies to every home product
Both quasi-peak and average limits are on the log slope between their endpoints
explanation: 0.2 MHz is between 0.15 MHz and 0.5 MHz, so you are still on the slope. The flat rows start at 0.5 MHz.

stem: At 0.25 MHz, which Class B conducted statement is right?
choices: Both quasi-peak and average limits are on the log slope between their endpoints
Class A 73/60 applies to every home product
explanation: 0.25 MHz is between 0.15 MHz and 0.5 MHz, so you are still on the slope. The flat rows start at 0.5 MHz.

stem: At 0.4 MHz, which Class B conducted statement is right?
choices: Both quasi-peak and average limits are on the log slope between their endpoints
Class A 73/60 applies to every home product
explanation: 0.4 MHz is between 0.15 MHz and 0.5 MHz, so you are still on the slope. The flat rows start at 0.5 MHz.

stem: You can pass conducted emissions by reporting only the line that looks better.
explanation: Section 15.107 requires the voltage from each power line to ground. The worse line is part of the result.

stem: A quasi-peak reading under the average limit still needs a separate average scan.
explanation: EN 301 489-1 says that if quasi-peak already meets the average limit, the average measurement is unnecessary. Quasi-peak does not read lower than average.

stem: The CISPR 14-1 preview in this pack includes the full click-rate limit table.
explanation: The preview shows that discontinuous disturbances and a click analyser exist. It does not print the rate limits, so this quiz does not invent them.

stem: Class A conducted limits are what you use for a product marketed to the general public for home use.
explanation: A home product is Class B. Class A is the commercial table and the numbers are looser, and marketing for the home selects the Class B rows.

stem: The ICES-002 >75 kVA conducted limits are available to any large product with no installation conditions.
explanation: Note v requires a dedicated transformer or generator, separation from residences by 30 m or a barrier, and instructions that say so. Otherwise those numbers are not yours.

stem: Mains conducted emissions and radiated emissions are the same measurement.
explanation: One is a voltage on the mains port from 150 kHz to 30 MHz. The other is a field, usually from 30 MHz up, and passing one does not pass the other.

stem: An open unused LISN port is the condition the 50 Ω limit assumes.
explanation: The unused port is terminated in 50 Ω. Leaving it open changes the impedance the product is tested against.

stem: Flicker and voltage fluctuation for a radio up to 16 A per phase, with no conditional connection, follow:
explanation: Clause 8.6 of EN 301 489-1 points that case at EN 61000-3-3. Conditional connection, or current above 16 A up to 75 A, uses EN 61000-3-11, and neither test is the 150 kHz RF voltage scan.

stem: The CISPR receiver bandwidth you set for a 150 kHz to 30 MHz mains scan is:
explanation: Band B of CISPR 16-1-1 is 9 kHz across that range. 120 kHz is the band used higher up for quasi-peak radiated work, and 1 MHz is the above-1 GHz bandwidth.
